sections.section_title: From bite to bedside: initial presentation, sepsis, and early management
sections.description: Walks through the exposure history, early clinical deterioration, and initial sepsis-directed evaluation and therapy, with a focused review of Capnocytophaga canimorsus as the likely pathogen.
subtopics: Timeline: dog bite, no prophylactic antibiotics taken, high fever, hypoglycaemia, mottled extremities
Initial exam and labs: pancytopenia, lactic acidosis, AKI, transaminitis, coagulopathy; urinalysis with proteinuria and haematuria
Sepsis assessment and DIC: clinical rationale for diagnosing DIC and multiorgan involvement; qSOFA context
Early differential at presentation: necrotising soft tissue infection ruled out; acute leukaemia/HLH considered; flow cytometry normal
Empiric antimicrobials: rationale for piperacillin/tazobactam to cover dog-associated pathogens including Capnocytophaga
Microbiology of Capnocytophaga canimorsus: slow-growing, encapsulated gram-negative rod; culture delays; confirmation from blood cultures

ICU course and supportive care: progression to anuria, septic cardiomyopathy, initiation of continuous renal replacement therapy; blood product support; skin ecchymoses and distal ischaemic changes compatible with microthrombi

sections.section_title: Recognizing superimposed TMA: diagnostic pivot from resolving sepsis to CM-HUS
sections.description: Explains the inflection point when improving sepsis unmasked a thrombotic microangiopathy, and details the targeted workup that led to a clinicopathologic diagnosis of complement-mediated HUS.
subtopics: Clinical trigger for re-evaluation: sudden isolated haemoglobin drop with persistent thrombocytopenia despite improving infection and normalising coagulation
Laboratory hallmarks of MAHA: rising LDH, undetectable haptoglobin, absence of overt bleeding
Direct antiglobulin test pitfall: initial IgG positivity likely drug/transfusion-related; lack of steroid response; repeat DAT negative
Peripheral smear: 15%–20% schistocytes confirming MAHA
Distinguishing DIC from TMA: normalising PT/aPTT/fibrinogen while haemolysis and thrombocytopenia persist; organ-specific clues (AKI, skin microthrombi)
Rule-out testing: ADAMTS13 activity 43.5% (TTP unlikely); PLASMIC score 4/7; Shiga-toxin PCR negative (STEC-HUS unlikely)
Complement testing nuances: normal C3/C4 and pathway screens do not exclude CM-HUS; timing relative to PEX/eculizumab can confound results (low AH50 post-treatment)
Renal biopsy: acute tubular necrosis, ischaemic glomeruli with fibrin thrombi, scattered crescents; no immune complex deposition—findings consistent with TMA
Synthesis: diagnosis of CM-HUS as a clinicopathologic diagnosis of exclusion, infection-triggered after C. canimorsus bacteraemia

sections.section_title: Pathophysiology in focus: alternative complement pathway dysregulation and infectious triggers
sections.description: Provides the mechanistic framework necessary to understand CM-HUS, how infections trigger endothelial injury, and why standard complement tests can be misleading during acute illness.
subtopics: Alternative pathway regulation: roles of factor H, factor I, factor B, and membrane cofactor protein (CD46)
Endothelial injury cascade: unchecked C3/C5 activation, membrane attack complex formation, platelet activation, and microvascular thrombosis causing MAHA, thrombocytopenia, and AKI
Genetics and penetrance: variants/autoantibodies in ~50%–70% of cases with incomplete penetrance; need for a second hit
Why C3/C4 may be normal: complement consumption may be compartmentalised; serum levels lack sensitivity for CM-HUS
Capnocytophaga as a trigger: capsule-mediated partial complement resistance; paradox of complement-mediated bacterial clearance versus host endothelial damage
Case application: no pathogenic complement variants identified; infection-triggered CM-HUS without demonstrable inherited predisposition

sections.section_title: Therapeutic strategy and sequencing: balancing infection control with complement blockade
sections.description: Details the treatment priorities and rationale: when to use plasma exchange, when and how to start eculizumab, how to mitigate infectious risks, and how to monitor response.
subtopics: Immediate priorities: definitive antibiotics with de-escalation once cultures identify C. canimorsus; hemodynamic and renal support (CRRT)
PEX as bridge: initiated while excluding TTP and prior to complement blockade; expected transient improvement (diuresis returned after final PEX)
Eculizumab essentials: mechanism (C5 inhibition), induction and maintenance dosing (900 mg weekly ×4, then 1200 mg every 2 weeks), early initiation improves renal outcomes
Infection risk mitigation: initiate after negative blood cultures; MenACWY (Menveo) and MenB (Bexsero) vaccination; antibiotic prophylaxis when vaccines not given ≥2 weeks pre-therapy
Transfusion and adjuncts: RBC transfusions for anaemia; platelet and fibrinogen support as needed; discontinuing steroids once AIHA excluded
Monitoring therapeutic response: platelet recovery, LDH/haptoglobin normalisation, return of diuresis, creatinine trajectory, dialysis weaning
Therapy duration planning: integrate genetic results, disease severity, and relapse risk to guide taper/cessation; structured follow-up and patient education on relapse signs

sections.description: Summarises the patient’s course and distils practical lessons for clinicians managing suspected CM-HUS after sepsis or DIC.
subtopics: Outcome in this case: haematologic remission; partial renal recovery (creatinine ~175 µmol/L); off dialysis with ongoing eculizumab maintenance
Prognostic factors: baseline renal function, need for dialysis, and time-to-eculizumab initiation; genetic findings inform relapse risk and treatment duration

Operational diagnostic algorithm: in MAHA + thrombocytopenia ± AKI—send ADAMTS13 urgently and start PEX if TTP possible; test for STEC; consider CM-HUS when ADAMTS13 >10% and stool PCR negative; biopsy when safe; do not rely on C3/C4 alone; start eculizumab promptly once infection controlled

Common pitfalls and pearls: TMA can be obscured by early DIC; normal complement levels do not exclude CM-HUS; interpret complement assays cautiously after PEX/eculizumab; be alert to drug/transfusion-related false-positive DAT
Broader implications: recognise zoonotic triggers like C. canimorsus; ensure timely empiric coverage for animal-bite sepsis; leverage molecular diagnostics when cultures are delayed
